front: In an agentic loop, which field tells your code whether to run a tool or stop?
back: stop_reason: keep looping on "tool_use", stop on "end_turn". It is the model's own structured signal, so no guessing is needed. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.1 (Tier 1)

front: After your code runs a tool Claude asked for, what must happen before the next request?
back: Append the tool result to the conversation history. Claude can only reason about the next step from what is in its context. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.1 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Stop the loop when Claude's reply contains words like 'done' or 'finished'."
back: Parsing natural language to end the loop is a named anti-pattern. Use stop_reason, which is structured and reliable. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.1 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Set max iterations to 10 as the way the loop ends."
back: An arbitrary cap as the primary stopping rule cuts off real work or wastes turns. stop_reason ends the loop; a cap is only a safety net. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.1 (Tier 1)

front: Model-driven decision-making vs a pre-configured decision tree: what is the difference?
back: In an agent, Claude picks the next tool from context; a decision tree fixes the sequence in code. Agents fit open tasks; fixed trees fit predictable ones. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.1 (Tier 1)

front: What is hub-and-spoke in a multi-agent system?
back: A coordinator manages all communication, error handling and routing between subagents. Subagents never talk to each other directly, which keeps flow observable. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.2 (Tier 1)

front: Do subagents inherit the coordinator's conversation history?
back: No. Each subagent has isolated context and sees only what the coordinator passes it. Missing facts in its output usually mean missing facts in its prompt. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.2 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "A competitor analysis covered only pricing and skipped product and support, so give the web-search subagent a longer timeout."
back: If every subagent did what it was asked, the gap is upstream: the coordinator split the topic too narrowly. Fix the decomposition, not a subagent setting. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.2 (Tier 1)

front: Should a coordinator always route every query through the full subagent pipeline?
back: No. It should analyse the query and invoke only the subagents its complexity needs. Running the full pipeline every time wastes time and cost. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.2 (Tier 1)

front: How does a coordinator make sure a synthesized report has no coverage gaps?
back: An iterative refinement loop: evaluate the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate targeted queries to search and analysis subagents, re-run synthesis until coverage is enough. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.2 (Tier 1)

front: Which tool does a coordinator use to spawn a subagent, and what config must allow it?
back: Saved-guide wording: the coordinator uses the Task tool with "Task" in allowedTools for delegation. (Current runtime: the tool is `Agent` (renamed in Claude Code v2.1.63; `Task` still works as an alias), and `allowedTools` only pre-approves tools; see [exam answer vs today](deep-practice/conditions-and-errors.md#exam-answer-vs-today).) | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.3 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "The synthesis subagent ignores earlier findings, so raise its max_tokens."
back: The subagent never received those findings. Pass the complete prior outputs in its prompt; a token limit cannot supply context that was never sent. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.3 (Tier 1)

front: How do you pass findings between agents without losing which source said what?
back: Use a structured format that separates content from metadata (URL, document name, page). Attribution then survives each hand-off. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.3 (Tier 1)

front: How do you run three subagents in parallel?
back: Emit three Task tool calls in one coordinator response. Spreading them across separate turns makes them sequential. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.3 (Tier 1)

front: Should a coordinator's prompt to a subagent give step-by-step procedure or goals?
back: Goals and quality criteria. Procedural scripts stop the subagent adapting to what it finds. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.3 (Tier 1)

front: Why can't a system prompt alone guarantee an account-ownership check happens before a SIM swap?
back: Prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate. When compliance must be deterministic, enforce the order in code with a prerequisite gate. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.4 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Add 'ALWAYS verify identity first' in capitals to the system prompt."
back: Louder wording is still a request the model can skip. A programmatic prerequisite that blocks the downstream tool until verification returns is a guarantee. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.4 (Tier 1)

front: What does a programmatic prerequisite gate do?
back: It blocks a downstream tool call (e.g. close_account) until the prerequisite step has returned the needed value (e.g. a verified account-holder ID). | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.4 (Tier 1)

front: What goes in a handoff summary when an agent escalates to a human?
back: Customer ID, root cause, amounts, and the recommended action, in a structured summary. The human usually cannot see the transcript. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.4 (Tier 1)

front: A customer raises three separate problems in one message. What is the pattern?
back: Split them into distinct items, investigate each (in parallel where possible) with shared context, then synthesize one unified resolution. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.4 (Tier 1)

front: What does a PostToolUse hook let you do?
back: Intercept a tool result and transform it (e.g. normalize timestamps or status codes) before the model processes it. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.5 (Tier 1)

front: Which kind of hook blocks a credit-limit increase above a set amount?
back: A PreToolUse hook: it intercepts the outgoing tool call before it runs and blocks or redirects it, e.g. to human approval. It runs in code every time. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.5 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "MCP tools return dates in three formats, so tell Claude in the prompt to convert them all to ISO 8601."
back: That relies on the model getting it right every time. A PostToolUse hook normalizes the data deterministically before Claude sees it. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.5 (Tier 1)

front: Hooks vs prompt instructions: which gives deterministic guarantees?
back: Hooks. Prompt instructions are probabilistic compliance. Choose hooks when a business rule must always hold. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.5 (Tier 1)

front: When do you pick prompt chaining over dynamic decomposition?
back: Prompt chaining (fixed sequential steps) for predictable multi-aspect work; dynamic decomposition when later subtasks depend on what you discover. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.6 (Tier 1)

front: How should a large multi-file code review be decomposed?
back: Per-file local analysis passes, then a separate cross-file integration pass. One pass over everything dilutes attention. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.6 (Tier 1)

front: How do you decompose an open task like "add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase"?
back: Map the structure first, find high-impact areas, then build a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.6 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "For an open-ended investigation, write the full list of subtasks up front so the run is predictable."
back: Open-ended work needs an adaptive plan that generates subtasks from findings. A fixed list misses what you only learn mid-investigation. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.6 (Tier 1)

front: How do you continue a specific earlier Claude Code investigation?
back: --resume <session-name> continues that named session with its prior context (name a session with -n or /rename). | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.7 (Tier 1)

front: What is fork_session for?
back: Creating independent branches from a shared analysis baseline, e.g. to compare two refactoring approaches without re-doing the analysis. fork_session is an Agent SDK option (Python fork_session=True, TypeScript forkSession: true); the CLI equivalent is --fork-session with --resume or --continue. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.7 (Tier 1)

front: Resume or start fresh? When is a new session with a summary better?
back: When the earlier tool results are stale (files changed a lot). A fresh session with an injected structured summary beats resuming on outdated context. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.7 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "After editing two files, resume the session and ask Claude to re-explore the whole repo."
back: Wasteful. Resume and tell the agent exactly which files changed so it re-analyses only those. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 1.7 (Tier 1)

front: What is the main thing Claude uses to choose between tools?
back: The tool descriptions. Minimal or overlapping descriptions cause unreliable selection among similar tools. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.1 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Claude keeps picking the wrong one of two similar tools, so lower the temperature."
back: Sampling settings do not fix ambiguous descriptions. Rewrite the descriptions (purpose, inputs, outputs, when to use vs the other tool) or rename them. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.1 (Tier 1)

front: What belongs in a good tool description?
back: Purpose, input formats, example queries, edge cases, outputs and boundaries: when to use it versus similar tools. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.1 (Tier 1)

front: Two tools, analyze_content and analyze_document, are misrouted because their names overlap. What is the rename fix?
back: Rename to remove the overlap (e.g. analyze_content becomes extract_web_results) and give it a web-specific description. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.1 (Tier 1)

front: One generic tool does several jobs and Claude uses it for the wrong one. What is the split fix?
back: Split it into purpose-specific tools, each with a clear input/output contract and its own description. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.1 (Tier 1)

front: How can a system prompt break good tool descriptions?
back: Keyword-sensitive instructions ("whenever the user says 'order', check the customer") create unintended tool associations. Review the prompt for them. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.1 (Tier 1)

front: What is the MCP isError flag for?
back: Telling the agent a tool call failed, so it can decide how to recover instead of treating the output as data. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.2 (Tier 1)

front: Name the four error categories the guide distinguishes.
back: Transient (timeout, unavailable), validation (bad input), business (policy violation) and permission. Each needs a different recovery. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.2 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Return a simple 'Operation failed' for every error to keep the tool interface clean."
back: Uniform errors stop the agent choosing a sensible recovery. Return errorCategory, isRetryable and a readable description. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.2 (Tier 1)

front: Why include isRetryable: false on a business-rule error?
back: It prevents wasted retries and, with a customer-friendly explanation, lets the agent tell the user what is going on. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.2 (Tier 1)

front: A search returns zero results. Is that an error?
back: No, if the query succeeded: it is a valid empty result. An access failure (timeout) is different and needs a retry decision. Report them differently. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.2 (Tier 1)

front: What happens to tool selection when an agent has 18 tools instead of 4-5?
back: Reliability drops because the decision gets harder. Give each agent only the tools its role needs. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.3 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "The synthesis agent keeps running web searches, so tell it in the prompt not to search."
back: Remove the search tool from that agent. Tools outside an agent's specialization get misused; scoping tool access is the design fix. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.3 (Tier 1)

front: What are the tool_choice options?
back: "auto" (may answer in text), "any" (must call some tool), and forced {"type": "tool", "name": "..."} (must call that tool). (Exam wording. Today `any` and forced `tool` return 400 on the models listed in the forced-tool-use table in Define tools (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools, checked 2026-10-21): see [exam answer vs today](deep-practice/conditions-and-errors.md#exam-answer-vs-today).) | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.3 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "To make sure extract_metadata runs first, write 'call extract_metadata first' in the prompt."
back: That is a request, not a guarantee. Force it with tool_choice {"type":"tool","name":"extract_metadata"}, then handle later steps in follow-up turns. (Exam wording. Today forced `tool` returns 400 on the models listed in the forced-tool-use table in Define tools (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools, checked 2026-10-21): see [exam answer vs today](deep-practice/conditions-and-errors.md#exam-answer-vs-today).) | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.3 (Tier 1)

front: A synthesis agent often needs quick fact checks. Give it the full search agent's tools?
back: No. Give a scoped cross-role tool (e.g. verify_fact) for the frequent simple case and route complex cases through the coordinator. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.3 (Tier 1)

front: Where do you configure an MCP server the whole team should get?
back: Project-level .mcp.json in the repo (shared via version control). Personal or experimental servers go in user-level ~/.claude.json. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.4 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Paste the GitHub token into .mcp.json so teammates' servers work."
back: Never commit secrets. Use environment variable expansion such as ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in .mcp.json. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.4 (Tier 1)

front: What are MCP resources good for?
back: Exposing content catalogs (issue summaries, doc trees, schemas) so the agent sees what exists without exploratory tool calls. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.4 (Tier 1)

front: Claude prefers built-in Grep over your more capable MCP search tool. Fix?
back: Improve the MCP tool's description to explain its capabilities and outputs in detail. Selection follows descriptions. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.4 (Tier 1)

front: Grep or Glob: which finds all callers of a function?
back: Grep, because it searches file contents. Glob matches file paths by name pattern (e.g. **/*.test.tsx). | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.5 (Tier 1)

front: Edit fails because the anchor text is not unique. What now?
back: Read the full file, then Write the corrected version. Read + Write is the reliable fallback. (Today Edit can also take `replace_all: true` when every match should change. On the exam, the fallback is Read + Write.) | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.5 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "To understand a new codebase, Read every file first."
back: Build understanding incrementally: Grep for entry points, then Read to follow imports and trace flows. Reading everything floods context. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 2.5 (Tier 1)

front: Name the three CLAUDE.md levels.
back: User (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project (.claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md), and directory (subdirectory CLAUDE.md). | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.1 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "A new teammate isn't getting our conventions, so tell them to run with a higher-effort setting."
back: The conventions are probably in someone's user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which is not shared. Move them to project-level CLAUDE.md in the repo. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.1 (Tier 1)

front: How do you keep CLAUDE.md modular?
back: Use @import to pull in specific standards files, or split topics into files under .claude/rules/ (testing.md, api-conventions.md...). | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.1 (Tier 1)

front: Which command shows which memory files are actually loaded?
back: /memory. Use it to diagnose inconsistent behaviour across sessions. (Exam answer. Today `/memory` lists memory file locations; `/context` lists, under Memory files, the CLAUDE.md files loaded at launch. A path-scoped rule or a subfolder CLAUDE.md loads later, and the terminal shows a "Loaded …" line when it does.) | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.1 (Tier 1)

front: Where does a slash command go so every developer gets it on clone?
back: Project .claude/commands/ (in version control). ~/.claude/commands/ is personal only. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.2 (Tier 1)

front: What does context: fork do in a skill's SKILL.md frontmatter?
back: Runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so verbose or exploratory output does not pollute the main conversation. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.2 (Tier 1)

front: Name two other skill frontmatter fields from the guide and their jobs.
back: allowed-tools restricts which tools the skill may use; argument-hint prompts the developer for required parameters. (Exam guide wording. In current Claude Code, allowed-tools pre-approves tools and disallowed-tools removes them. See [exam answer vs today](deep-practice/conditions-and-errors.md#exam-answer-vs-today).) | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.2 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Put a rarely used 200-line release workflow into CLAUDE.md so it's always available."
back: CLAUDE.md is always loaded and meant for universal standards. Task-specific workflows belong in a skill, invoked on demand. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.2 (Tier 1)

front: How do you make a rule load only when Claude edits Terraform files?
back: A file in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter paths: ["terraform/**/*"]. It loads only for matching files. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.3 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Test files live next to source everywhere, so add a CLAUDE.md to every directory with test rules."
back: A path-scoped rule with a glob like **/*.test.tsx applies to matching files wherever they live. Directory CLAUDE.md files can't follow files across folders. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.3 (Tier 1)

front: Why do path-scoped rules save tokens?
back: They load only when matching files are edited, so irrelevant conventions stay out of context. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.3 (Tier 1)

front: Rules in .claude/rules/ vs subdirectory CLAUDE.md: which for conventions spread across the codebase?
back: Path-specific rules with glob patterns. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md suits conventions tied to one directory. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.3 (Tier 1)

front: When should you use plan mode?
back: Large-scale or multi-file changes, several valid approaches, architectural decisions (e.g. a library migration touching 45+ files). | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.4 (Tier 1)

front: When is direct execution right?
back: Simple, well-scoped changes: a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace, adding one validation check. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.4 (Tier 1)

front: What is the Explore subagent for?
back: Isolating verbose discovery output and returning a summary, so the main conversation's context is preserved. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.4 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "A big migration keeps running out of context, so switch to a model with a bigger window."
back: Fix the design: plan mode for investigation, the Explore subagent for verbose discovery, then direct execution of the planned approach. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.4 (Tier 1)

front: Prose instructions for a transformation give inconsistent results. Best fix?
back: Give 2-3 concrete input/output examples. Examples communicate the transformation better than prose. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.5 (Tier 1)

front: What is the interview pattern?
back: Have Claude ask you questions before implementing, to surface considerations (cache invalidation, failure modes) you had not anticipated. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.5 (Tier 1)

front: Several bugs to fix. One message or one at a time?
back: One detailed message when the fixes interact; sequential iteration when they are independent. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.5 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "The migration script mishandles nulls, so tell Claude to 'be more careful with edge cases'."
back: Give a specific test case with example input and expected output. Test-driven iteration with shared failures is the reliable fix. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.5 (Tier 1)

front: Your CI job hangs waiting for input. What flag fixes it?
back: -p (--print) runs Claude Code non-interactively. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.6 (Tier 1)

front: How do you get machine-parseable findings from Claude Code in CI?
back: --output-format json with --json-schema, so results can be posted as inline PR comments. --json-schema works only in print mode (-p). (Flags: check the current docs.) | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.6 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "In the same session that wrote the code, ask Claude to review its own changes critically."
back: The generating session keeps its reasoning and is less likely to question itself. Use an independent review instance. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.6 (Tier 1)

front: Re-running a CI review after new commits produces duplicate comments. Fix?
back: Include the prior findings in context and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 3.6 (Tier 1)

front: Why do explicit criteria beat "be conservative"?
back: Vague confidence instructions do not improve precision. Specific categorical criteria (report X, skip Y) do. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.1 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Too many false positives, so add 'only report high-confidence findings'."
back: Confidence-based filtering fails. Define which issue types to report and which to skip, with concrete examples per severity. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.1 (Tier 1)

front: One review category has a very high false-positive rate. What do you do while you fix it?
back: Temporarily disable that category to restore developer trust, then improve its prompt. Bad categories undermine trust in good ones. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.1 (Tier 1)

front: How do you get consistent severity labels?
back: Define explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each level. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.1 (Tier 1)

front: Detailed instructions still give inconsistent output format. Most effective fix?
back: Few-shot examples showing the exact format (location, issue, severity, fix). | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.2 (Tier 1)

front: How many few-shot examples, and of what?
back: 2-4 targeted examples of ambiguous cases, showing the reasoning for why one action beats plausible alternatives. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.2 (Tier 1)

front: Can few-shot examples help Claude handle cases you did not list?
back: Yes. Good examples let the model generalize the judgment to novel patterns, not just match listed cases. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.2 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Extraction returns null for fields that exist in odd layouts, so make the fields required."
back: Required fields push the model to invent values. Add few-shot examples showing correct extraction from the varied formats. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.2 (Tier 1)

front: Most reliable way to get schema-compliant JSON from Claude?
back: Tool use with a JSON schema as the tool's input; read the tool_use block. This removes JSON syntax errors. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.3 (Tier 1)

front: Several extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown. tool_choice?
back: "any": Claude must call one of the extraction tools, and picks which. (Exam wording. Today `any` returns 400 on the models listed in the forced-tool-use table in Define tools (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools, checked 2026-10-21): see [exam answer vs today](deep-practice/conditions-and-errors.md#exam-answer-vs-today).) | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.3 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Strict schemas via tool use mean the extracted numbers are correct."
back: Schemas stop syntax errors, not semantic ones (line items not summing, values in the wrong field). You still validate in code. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.3 (Tier 1)

front: A field may be missing from the source document. Required or optional?
back: Optional (nullable), so the model is not pushed to fabricate a value. Add "unclear" and "other" + detail for categories. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.3 (Tier 1)

front: What should a retry request contain?
back: The original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors, so the model can correct itself. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.4 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Retry the extraction three more times; the missing contract date will turn up."
back: If the fact is not in the document (e.g. it is in an external file not provided), retries cannot help. Retries fix format and structure errors. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.4 (Tier 1)

front: How do you catch invoices whose line items don't add up?
back: Extract calculated_total alongside stated_total and flag differences; add a conflict_detected boolean for inconsistent sources. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.4 (Tier 1)

front: What is a detected_pattern field for?
back: Recording which code construct triggered a finding, so you can analyse which patterns developers keep dismissing. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.4 (Tier 1)

front: Message Batches API: three facts the guide gives.
back: 50% cost savings, up to a 24-hour processing window, no guaranteed latency SLA. (Pricing: check the current docs.) | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.5 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Move the blocking pre-merge check to batches to save 50%."
back: Batches suit latency-tolerant work (overnight, weekly). Blocking workflows stay on the synchronous API. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.5 (Tier 1)

front: Can a batch request do multi-turn tool calling?
back: Not a client-side loop: a batch request cannot pause for your code to run a tool and return its result, so those loops need the synchronous API. Batches do support tools, including server tools (tools Anthropic runs for you, such as web search) (Anthropic docs, Message Batches, Tier 1, checked 2026-10-12). | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.5 (Tier 1)

front: Some documents in a batch failed. What do you resubmit?
back: Only the failed ones, found by custom_id, with fixes (e.g. chunk documents that were too long). | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.5 (Tier 1)

front: Why is self-review in the same session weak?
back: The model keeps its generation reasoning and is less likely to question its own decisions. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.6 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Turn on extended thinking so the generator reviews its own code more deeply."
back: An independent instance without the generator's reasoning context catches more than self-review or extended thinking. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.6 (Tier 1)

front: A single review pass over many files gives shallow and contradictory feedback. Design fix?
back: Per-file local passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass for data flow. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.6 (Tier 1)

front: What does a verification pass with per-finding confidence enable?
back: Calibrated review routing: low-confidence findings go to closer review. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 4.6 (Tier 1)

front: What is the risk of progressive summarization in long support chats?
back: Exact numbers, dates, percentages and customer expectations get condensed into vague text. Keep them in a persistent "case facts" block outside the summary. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.1 (Tier 1)

front: What is the "lost in the middle" effect and one mitigation?
back: Models handle the start and end of long inputs best. Put a key-findings summary at the start and use clear section headers. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.1 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Order lookups return 40 fields and context fills up, so raise max_tokens."
back: max_tokens limits output, not input bloat. Trim tool outputs to the relevant fields before they accumulate in context. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.1 (Tier 1)

front: Name the three appropriate escalation triggers.
back: The customer asks for a human; policy has an exception or gap; the agent cannot make meaningful progress. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.2 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Escalate when sentiment analysis shows the customer is angry."
back: Sentiment and self-reported confidence are unreliable proxies for complexity. Use explicit criteria, and always honour an explicit request for a human. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.2 (Tier 1)

front: A customer says "I want a human" on a simple issue. What does the agent do?
back: Hand off immediately, without investigating first. Only if they are frustrated but did not ask does the agent offer to resolve, escalating if they repeat the request. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.2 (Tier 1)

front: A lookup returns three customers named Lee. What does the agent do?
back: Ask for another identifier. Never pick one by heuristic. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.2 (Tier 1)

front: What should a subagent's error report to the coordinator include?
back: Failure type, what was attempted, partial results and possible alternatives. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.3 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "If a source times out, return an empty list so the workflow keeps going."
back: Silently turning failures into empty success hides them. Report the access failure with context; empty means the query worked and found nothing. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.3 (Tier 1)

front: Should a subagent pass every transient failure up to the coordinator?
back: No. Retry transient failures locally; propagate only what it cannot resolve, with what was tried and partial results. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.3 (Tier 1)

front: In a long exploration Claude starts citing "typical patterns" instead of the classes it found. What is happening?
back: Context degradation. Counter it with scratchpad files of key findings, subagents for verbose searches, and /compact. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.4 (Tier 1)

front: How do you design crash recovery for a multi-agent exploration?
back: Each agent exports structured state to a known location; the coordinator loads a manifest on resume and injects it into agent prompts. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.4 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Keep all exploration in one main session so nothing is lost."
back: Verbose output degrades the main context. Delegate specific questions to subagents and keep the main agent on coordination. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.4 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "Overall extraction accuracy is 97%, so remove human review."
back: An aggregate can hide poor results on specific document types or fields. Measure accuracy per type and field first. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.5 (Tier 1)

front: How do you keep measuring errors in high-confidence extractions after automating?
back: Stratified random sampling of those extractions, which also surfaces new error patterns. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.5 (Tier 1)

front: How do you make field-level confidence scores useful for routing?
back: Calibrate the review thresholds against a labeled validation set; route low-confidence or contradictory items to humans. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.5 (Tier 1)

front: Two credible sources give different figures. What should the synthesis do?
back: Include both, annotated with their sources. Do not pick one arbitrarily. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.6 (Tier 1)

front: TRAP: Tempting wrong answer: "A 2021 and a 2025 figure disagree, so flag a contradiction."
back: They may just be different periods. Require publication or collection dates in subagent outputs so time differences are read correctly. | Source: CCAR-F exam guide v1.0, section 6, task statement 5.6 (Tier 1)
